transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess the main thing is that I just can’t seem to keep my work in order anymore. I work with laundry and dry cleaning, so there are tickets and receipts and notes from the workshop, and then customer jobs that need to be tracked, and it all just ends up piled together. I’ll have one stack that was supposed to be “to do,” another stack that was supposed to be “finished,” and then somehow receipts or little notes get mixed in, and before I know it I’m standing there not knowing what I’m supposed to handle first.

It’s embarrassing, honestly, because it feels like I should be able to keep simple things straight, but lately it’s like the more I try to sort it, the more confused I get. That’s really what brought me in.
How long have you been experiencing this difficulty with keeping your work organized?

It’s been really causing trouble for, I’d say, a little over two years now — about two years and maybe two months. It wasn’t like one day everything fell apart all at once, but that’s when I started changing the business into more of this boutique kind of model, where it wasn’t just the regular laundry and dry cleaning routine anymore. There were more special orders, more little details to keep track of, different kinds of customer notes, and it just got more complicated.

Before that I could sort of muddle through with my usual piles and reminders, even if it wasn’t perfect. But since making those changes, the organizing part has become a real problem, not just an annoyance. That’s when it started actually interfering with the work in a way I couldn’t just brush off.
Have you been feeling anxious or overwhelmed by your work situation?

I mean… overwhelmed, yes, in the sense that when I’m looking at all the tickets and bags and notes, it feels like too much at once. But I don’t know if I’d call it anxious exactly. I’m not sure what counts as anxiety, really.

It’s more like I get stuck. I’ll stand there thinking, “Okay, start with this pile,” and then I see something else that should have been done yesterday, or a customer receipt that doesn’t seem to match what’s on the bag, and then my head just gets full. I feel frustrated and embarrassed, and sometimes I sort of freeze because I don’t know which thing to fix first.

So… yes, overwhelmed by the work situation, definitely. Anxious maybe, but I’m not sure if that’s the right word for it.
Do you have difficulty focusing on a single task for an extended period of time?

Yes, I do. That’s actually one of the things that drives me crazy, because I can start out meaning to do one very simple thing, like go over the day’s dry-cleaning orders and make sure the tickets match the bags, and at first I’m fine. I’ll have the papers in front of me, I know what I’m supposed to be checking, and I’ll tell myself, “Just go down the list.”

But after a few minutes, it’s like my mind just slips away. I’ll be looking at a label and then suddenly I’m thinking about some other label that was wrong last week, or something I need to do for choir, or something at home that I forgot to handle. And then I look back down and realize I don’t actually remember the last several orders I supposedly checked.

So it’s not that I don’t care or that I’m trying to avoid it. I really am trying to stay with the one task. But keeping my mind on it for any length of time is hard, and then I have to go back and recheck things because I don’t trust that I caught everything the first time.
Do you have trouble remembering things that happened recently?

I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I don’t think I have, like, whole recent events disappearing from my mind, if that’s what you mean. If something happened yesterday or earlier in the week, usually I can remember it once someone gives me the context.

But sometimes I’ll have to stop and think, like, “Wait, did that customer come in this morning or was that yesterday?” or “Did I already tell someone about that?” So I don’t know if that counts as trouble remembering recent things, or if it’s more just everything blurring together when the days are busy.

I haven’t noticed it as a big separate problem the way some other things feel like problems. It’s more that I might need a reminder or a minute to place it.
Have you noticed any problems in your personal relationships or daily life outside of work because of these difficulties with organization and focus?

Yes… unfortunately, yes. It’s not only at work anymore, or maybe work is where it shows the most because everything has to be tracked and matched and finished on time, but it spills over.

At the shop, there have been late orders because I thought something was already handled or I didn’t keep the steps straight. And then the billing gets confused sometimes, like a customer’s ticket doesn’t seem to match what I thought we charged, or there’s a note somewhere but not where it should be. That creates these tense moments with the other staff, because they’re trying to help or they’re asking me what happened, and I honestly don’t always have a clean answer. Then with customers, it’s embarrassing, because they just want their clothes and a clear bill, and I’m standing there trying to sort out what went wrong.

Outside of work, church is the main place I notice it. I used to help more with planning things, like organizing details and keeping track of who was doing what, but I’ve stepped back from some of that. Not because I don’t care — I do care — but people were getting frustrated with me. I’d miss a piece of information or not follow through in the right order, and then someone else would have to chase it down. After a while I could feel that I was making things harder, so I pulled back. That felt pretty bad, honestly.
Do you find that your mood changes frequently throughout the day?

I’m not sure I’d say my mood changes a lot throughout the day, not in a way I’ve really been keeping track of. I mean, I can get frustrated or embarrassed when something goes wrong, and then if it gets straightened out I may calm down again, but I don’t know if that’s the same thing as mood changing frequently.

It doesn’t feel to me like I’m going from happy to sad to angry for no reason all day long. It’s more that my mood reacts to what’s happening around me, if that makes sense. If the day is going smoothly, I’m usually okay. If things pile up or someone is upset with me, then I feel tense or down on myself. But I haven’t noticed sudden mood shifts just out of nowhere.
Do you feel like your difficulties with organization and focus are significantly interfering with your ability to function effectively in your daily life or work?

Yes, I do. I think I was trying not to make it sound too dramatic, but if I’m being honest, it really is getting in the way.

At the shop, it affects actual work getting done. We’ve had late orders because I didn’t keep track of the steps right or I thought something was already handled when it wasn’t. And the billing can get confused too — like there’s a ticket or a note, but then it doesn’t match up with what I remember, and then everybody’s trying to figure out what happened. That can turn into tense moments with the other staff, because they need a clear answer and I’m standing there trying to piece it together. And with customers it’s worse, because they’re waiting on their clothes or asking about a bill, and I feel embarrassed and kind of exposed.

It’s not just work either. At church, I’ve stepped back from helping lead some planning things. I used to be more involved with organizing details, but people were getting frustrated with me because I’d miss something or not follow through the way I was supposed to. I don’t want to be the person who makes extra work for everyone else, so I’ve backed off.

So yes, I’d say it’s interfering. Not every single minute of every day, but enough that it’s affecting my work and what I feel able to take on outside of work.
Do you feel distressed or upset by your difficulties with organization and focus?

Yes, I do. I get pretty upset about it, honestly. It’s not just that I misplace a paper or forget a small thing and then move on. It turns into real problems, and then I feel like I’ve let people down.

At the shop, when an order is late because I didn’t keep the steps straight, or I thought something was already taken care of and it wasn’t, I feel terrible. And the billing mix-ups are really stressful, because then it’s not just me being disorganized in private — it’s right there in front of coworkers or customers. Someone is asking, “What happened with this ticket?” or “Why doesn’t this match?” and I’m trying to remember where the note went or what I meant to do, and I can feel everyone getting tense. I don’t like being the reason the day gets harder for everyone else.

And at church, that’s been upsetting in a different way. I used to help more with planning, and I cared about doing that, but I stepped back because people were getting frustrated with me. I’d miss details or not follow through the way they expected, and then someone else would have to fix it or remind me. That made me feel embarrassed and kind of ashamed, like maybe I shouldn’t volunteer for things even when I want to help.

So yes, it bothers me a lot. I try to act like I’m handling it, but inside I’m often frustrated with myself.
Do you have trouble with making decisions or solving problems in your daily life?

Yes… I mean, maybe not decisions like what to eat for dinner, but at work, yes. When everything is piled up together, I have a hard time figuring out what to do first or how to sort it out.

That’s really part of what brought me in. I can’t seem to keep my work in order anymore. There will be tickets, receipts, workshop notes, and customer jobs all mixed together, and I’ll look at the whole mess and sort of freeze because I don’t know where to start. I’ll think, okay, I should handle this customer job first, but then I see a receipt that maybe needs matching to something, and then there’s a note from the workshop, and then I’m not sure if I already did part of it or just meant to do it.

So solving the problem becomes harder than it should be. It’s not that I don’t understand the work. I’ve done this kind of work a long time. It’s more like once the information is scattered and piled together, I can’t make a clean decision about the next step. I end up shuffling papers or going back and forth instead of just moving through it. And then the longer I take, the more behind I feel, and it gets even harder to decide what needs my attention first.
Do you find that you get mentally tired more easily than you used to, especially when trying to concentrate on tasks?

Yes, I do. It’s like I can sit down and start the day’s dry-cleaning orders okay — at first I’m looking at the tickets and checking what needs to be done, and I feel like, alright, I’m going to get through this properly. But then after just a few minutes, my mind has wandered off somewhere else.

Sometimes I’ll notice I’m thinking about the labels on the garments, or something with choir plans, or something I need to do at home, and then I kind of snap back and realize I missed half of what I was supposed to be checking. And it’s tiring because I have to go back over it again, but then I’m already frustrated with myself, so it feels harder to concentrate the second time.

It’s not that the work is new to me. I know how to do it. But keeping my mind on one run of orders all the way through feels like it takes more effort than it should, and I get worn out from trying to pull myself back over and over.
Do you find that you often forget things that you were supposed to do or remember?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that. I mean, I know I’ve been having trouble keeping track of things in general, but if you mean do I forget whole things I’m supposed to do, like appointments or promises, I’d have to think about it.

Sometimes it feels less like a clean “I forgot” and more like things just don’t stay in the right place in my head. I’ll have a sense that there was something I needed to take care of, but I can’t always put my finger on what it was right away. Or I’ll be sure I had something in mind, and then once I’m in the middle of something else, it slips away. But I don’t know if I can give you a neat list of examples off the top of my head.

So… yes, maybe at times, but I’m not sure how often, and I don’t want to overstate it. It’s more that I feel like I’m always trying to keep hold of things before they disappear on me.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain tasks or situations because they might exacerbate your difficulties with organization and focus?

I’m not sure. I don’t think I’d say I avoid them on purpose, exactly. It’s more that if I know something is going to involve a lot of sorting or keeping several things straight at once, I can feel myself kind of hesitate before starting it.

Like, I don’t wake up thinking, “I’m going to avoid this today,” but I might keep circling around it, doing little easier things first, or telling myself I’ll handle it once I get a clearer moment. And then sometimes that clearer moment doesn’t really come. But I don’t know if that counts as avoiding, or if it’s just me getting stuck before I start.

I guess I’ve noticed I’m more reluctant with anything that looks messy from the beginning. If things are already spread out or mixed together, I know it’s going to take a lot out of me, so I might put it off without really admitting that’s what I’m doing. But I wouldn’t say I’m avoiding whole situations in a big way. It’s more subtle than that, I think.
Have you noticed any problems in your personal relationships outside of work and church because of your difficulties with organization and focus?

I’m not really sure that I’ve noticed that, honestly. Outside of work and church… I mean, I don’t know that I have a clear example where someone in my personal life has said, “You’re so disorganized,” or where a relationship has really been affected because of it.

I suppose there are times I feel scattered just in general, and maybe that could spill over into conversations or making plans, but I can’t point to anything specific and say, yes, that caused a problem with a friend or family member. It’s not something that stands out to me the way the work things do.

So I’d say… not that I’ve clearly noticed. If you mean smaller annoyances, maybe I’d have to think more, but I don’t want to make it sound like there’s been some big relationship issue from it.
Do you feel like your brain gets tired more quickly than it used to when you're trying to think or concentrate?

Yes, I think so, though I don’t know if I would have described it as “tired” at first. It’s more like my mind starts out okay, and then it just sort of drifts off before I realize it.

Like at the dry-cleaning place, I can sit down or stand there and start going over the day’s orders just fine. I’ll be checking what needs to be done, matching things up, looking at the tags or the labels, and for the first few minutes I feel like, okay, I’m doing it. But then somehow my mind has wandered off to something else — maybe I’m thinking about a label on one garment, and then that reminds me of something else, or I start thinking about choir plans, or something I need to handle at home. And then I come back to what I’m supposed to be doing and realize I’ve missed half of what I was supposed to check.

So it’s not always that I feel sleepy or physically exhausted. It’s more that concentrating doesn’t hold the way I expect it to. I’ll think I’m following along, but then I notice I’ve been somewhere else in my head. And that does feel tiring, because then I have to go back and re-check things, and I’m never quite sure what I actually took in and what I only thought I took in.
Do you feel like you're unable to think clearly or make decisions after a period of mental effort?

Yes, I think that’s a fair way to put it, though for me it feels less like I suddenly can’t think at all and more like everything gets kind of… slippery. Like I can start out with the dry-cleaning orders and be perfectly able to follow what I’m supposed to do. I’ll be looking at the tickets, checking what’s come in, what needs to be matched up, what’s ready, what still needs attention — and at the beginning I feel like I’m clear enough.

But after a few minutes, it’s like my mind doesn’t stay with it. I’ll be looking at a label, and then that label makes me think of something else, or my mind jumps to choir plans, or something I’m supposed to do at home, and I don’t always notice right away that I’ve left the task in my head. Then I sort of come back and realize I’ve missed half of what I was supposed to be checking.

That’s when decisions get harder, because I’m not sure what I actually already looked at and what I only thought I looked at. So I might have to go back over the same order again, and then I get more unsure because now I’m trying to remember, “Did I check this already? Did I match that up right?” It’s not that I don’t know how to do the work. It’s that after holding my attention on it for a bit, my thinking doesn’t feel as clean or steady.
Have you noticed your difficulties with organization and focus affecting your relationships with family or friends?

I honestly don’t know that I can say yes to that in any clear way. With family or friends, I can’t think of someone telling me, you know, “You never pay attention,” or “Your organization is causing problems between us,” or anything like that.

I mean, I’m sure I have moments where I’m a little scattered or where I’m not as on top of things as I’d like to be, but I don’t have a specific relationship problem that comes to mind. It’s easier for me to notice it in more structured settings, where there are tasks and things that have to be done a certain way. With family and friends, it’s a little more vague, I guess.

So… no, not that I’ve really noticed. If it’s happening in small ways, maybe I’m not picking up on it, but I wouldn’t want to say it’s been a major issue because I don’t really have an example of that.
Have you felt like your difficulties with organization and focus have significantly affected your ability to maintain or deepen relationships with friends or family?

I don’t think I can really say that it has, at least not in a significant way. I mean, when you say “maintain or deepen relationships,” that sounds like a pretty big thing, like losing friends or not being close to family because I can’t stay organized or focused, and I don’t really have an example like that.

With work tasks, it’s easier for me to see where I get scattered, because there are orders and labels and steps, and if I lose track, there’s something concrete that shows it. But with friends or family, it’s harder for me to measure. I still talk to people, I still show up in the ways I know how, and I can’t think of anyone saying I’ve pulled away or that I’m impossible to deal with because of being disorganized.

I’m not saying I’m perfect. I’m sure there are times I forget little things or I’m not as present as I should be, but I don’t know that I’d connect that to relationships not growing or falling apart. So… no, not that I’ve noticed in any clear or major way.
Have you felt like your difficulties with organization and focus have caused you significant distress or problems in your relationships with others?

Yes… when you put it that way, I think it has caused problems, more than I maybe wanted to admit at first. I was thinking mostly about family and friends before, but with “relationships with others,” that does include work and church, and that’s where I can see it more clearly.

At the shop, it has definitely created tension. If I lose track of an order or don’t keep the steps straight, then an order can end up late, or the billing can get confused, and then it’s not just some private mistake in my head — somebody else has to deal with it. A customer is upset, or a coworker is trying to figure out what I meant, or we’re all going back through something that should have been simple. And I feel awful when that happens, because I’m not trying to be careless. I’m trying to do it right, but when I get disorganized, it can make other people frustrated with me.

There have been tense moments with staff and customers because of that. Not constant screaming or anything like that, but you can feel it — people get short, or they’re watching me more closely, or I feel like I have to explain myself. And then I get embarrassed, because I know they need me to be dependable.

At church, too, I’ve stepped back from leading some planning things because people were getting frustrated with me. That was hard, because I care about being involved, and I like helping, but keeping all the planning details straight was becoming a problem. I could tell it was wearing on people, and I didn’t want to be the reason things got confusing or delayed.

So yes, I would say it’s caused distress. Maybe not so much in my closest family relationships, but with coworkers, customers, and people at church, yes — it has affected how comfortable I feel and how much responsibility I’m willing to take on.
Do you often feel sad or depressed because of your difficulties with organization and focus?

I’m not sure I’d call it sad or depressed, exactly. I mean, I do get upset with myself sometimes, and embarrassed, especially when I feel like I should have been able to keep something straight and I didn’t. There’s that feeling of, “Why can’t I just do this the way other people seem to do it?” But I don’t know if that rises to the level of feeling depressed.

It’s more like frustration, I guess. Or discouragement in the moment. If I make a mistake or things get disorganized, I can really stew on it for a while, and I feel bad because I don’t want people thinking I don’t care or that I’m not trying. But I wouldn’t say I’m walking around sad all the time because of it.

So… often sad or depressed? I don’t think so. Frustrated and disappointed in myself sometimes, yes. But depressed doesn’t feel like quite the right word for it.

At the shop, it affects actual work getting done. We’ve had late orders because I didn’t keep track of the steps right or I thought something was already handled when it wasn’t. And the billing can get confused too — like there’s a ticket or a note, but then it doesn’t match up with what I remember, and then everybody’s trying to figure out what happened. That can turn into tense moments with the other staff, because they need a clear answer and I’m standing there trying to piece it together. And with customers it’s worse, because they’re waiting on their clothes or asking about a bill, and I feel embarrassed and kind of exposed.

It’s not just work either. At church, I’ve stepped back from helping lead some planning things. I used to be more involved with organizing details, but people were getting frustrated with me because I’d miss something or not follow through the way I was supposed to. I don’t want to be the person who makes extra work for everyone else, so I’ve backed off.

So yes, I’d say it’s interfering. Not every single minute of every day, but enough that it’s affecting my work and what I feel able to take on outside of work.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient experiences significant distress due to their symptoms
doctor.question: Do you feel distressed or upset by your difficulties with organization and focus?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: The shop has had late orders, confused billing, and tense moments with staff and customers, and at church I have stepped back from leading some planning because people were getting frustrated with me.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether the organization and focus difficulties cause distress or upset, which is most directly related to the impact these symptoms have on daily functioning and wellbeing.

patient.answer:
Yes, I do. I get pretty upset about it, honestly. It’s not just that I misplace a paper or forget a small thing and then move on. It turns into real problems, and then I feel like I’ve let people down.

At the shop, when an order is late because I didn’t keep the steps straight, or I thought something was already taken care of and it wasn’t, I feel terrible. And the billing mix-ups are really stressful, because then it’s not just me being disorganized in private — it’s right there in front of coworkers or customers. Someone is asking, “What happened with this ticket?” or “Why doesn’t this match?” and I’m trying to remember where the note went or what I meant to do, and I can feel everyone getting tense. I don’t like being the reason the day gets harder for everyone else.

And at church, that’s been upsetting in a different way. I used to help more with planning, and I cared about doing that, but I stepped back because people were getting frustrated with me. I’d miss details or not follow through the way they expected, and then someone else would have to fix it or remind me. That made me feel embarrassed and kind of ashamed, like maybe I shouldn’t volunteer for things even when I want to help.

So yes, it bothers me a lot. I try to act like I’m handling it, but inside I’m often frustrated with myself.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences cognitive symptoms beyond attention and memory
doctor.question: Do you have trouble with making decisions or solving problems in your daily life?

target_item.name: Organization_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is I cannot seem to keep my work in order anymore, with tickets, receipts, workshop notes, and customer jobs all piled together until I do not know what to handle first.
target_item.reason: The question about difficulty making decisions or solving daily problems is most closely related to trouble organizing tasks and figuring out what to handle first in daily life and work.

patient.answer:
Yes… I mean, maybe not decisions like what to eat for dinner, but at work, yes. When everything is piled up together, I have a hard time figuring out what to do first or how to sort it out.

That’s really part of what brought me in. I can’t seem to keep my work in order anymore. There will be tickets, receipts, workshop notes, and customer jobs all mixed together, and I’ll look at the whole mess and sort of freeze because I don’t know where to start. I’ll think, okay, I should handle this customer job first, but then I see a receipt that maybe needs matching to something, and then there’s a note from the workshop, and then I’m not sure if I already did part of it or just meant to do it.

So solving the problem becomes harder than it should be. It’s not that I don’t understand the work. I’ve done this kind of work a long time. It’s more like once the information is scattered and piled together, I can’t make a clean decision about the next step. I end up shuffling papers or going back and forth instead of just moving through it. And then the longer I take, the more behind I feel, and it gets even harder to decide what needs my attention first.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences cognitive fatigue
doctor.question: Do you find that you get mentally tired more easily than you used to, especially when trying to concentrate on tasks?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: I can start going over the day's dry-cleaning orders just fine, but after a few minutes my mind is off on labels, choir plans, or something at home, and then I realize I missed half of what I was supposed to check.
target_item.reason: The question is most directly about becoming mentally tired while trying to concentrate, which relates to difficulty sustaining attention during tasks.

patient.answer:
Yes, I do. It’s like I can sit down and start the day’s dry-cleaning orders okay — at first I’m looking at the tickets and checking what needs to be done, and I feel like, alright, I’m going to get through this properly. But then after just a few minutes, my mind has wandered off somewhere else.

Sometimes I’ll notice I’m thinking about the labels on the garments, or something with choir plans, or something I need to do at home, and then I kind of snap back and realize I missed half of what I was supposed to be checking. And it’s tiring because I have to go back over it again, but then I’m already frustrated with myself, so it feels harder to concentrate the second time.

It’s not that the work is new to me. I know how to do it. But keeping my mind on one run of orders all the way through feels like it takes more effort than it should, and I get worn out from trying to pull myself back over and over.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant memory loss
doctor.question: Do you find that you often forget things that you were supposed to do or remember?

target_item.reason: The question is directly about being forgetful in daily activities, but the provided symptom profile does not include a specific forgetfulness item.

patient.answer:
I’m not completely sure how to answer that. I mean, I know I’ve been having trouble keeping track of things in general, but if you mean do I forget whole things I’m supposed to do, like appointments or promises, I’d have to think about it.

Sometimes it feels less like a clean “I forgot” and more like things just don’t stay in the right place in my head. I’ll have a sense that there was something I needed to take care of, but I can’t always put my finger on what it was right away. Or I’ll be sure I had something in mind, and then once I’m in the middle of something else, it slips away. But I don’t know if I can give you a neat list of examples off the top of my head.

So… yes, maybe at times, but I’m not sure how often, and I don’t want to overstate it. It’s more that I feel like I’m always trying to keep hold of things before they disappear on me.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of avoidance behaviors related to the patient's difficulties
doctor.question: Do you find yourself avoiding certain tasks or situations because they might exacerbate your difficulties with organization and focus?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about avoiding tasks or situations because they worsen organization and focus problems, which corresponds to avoidance of effortful tasks; that symptom is not included in the provided profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. I don’t think I’d say I avoid them on purpose, exactly. It’s more that if I know something is going to involve a lot of sorting or keeping several things straight at once, I can feel myself kind of hesitate before starting it.

Like, I don’t wake up thinking, “I’m going to avoid this today,” but I might keep circling around it, doing little easier things first, or telling myself I’ll handle it once I get a clearer moment. And then sometimes that clearer moment doesn’t really come. But I don’t know if that counts as avoiding, or if it’s just me getting stuck before I start.

I guess I’ve noticed I’m more reluctant with anything that looks messy from the beginning. If things are already spread out or mixed together, I know it’s going to take a lot out of me, so I might put it off without really admitting that’s what I’m doing. But I wouldn’t say I’m avoiding whole situations in a big way. It’s more subtle than that, I think.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in social relationships due to their symptoms
doctor.question: Have you noticed any problems in your personal relationships outside of work and church because of your difficulties with organization and focus?

target_item.reason: The question asks about impairment in personal relationships outside of work and church due to organization and focus problems, but the provided symptom profile only describes impairment at the shop and church, not other personal relationships.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure that I’ve noticed that, honestly. Outside of work and church… I mean, I don’t know that I have a clear example where someone in my personal life has said, “You’re so disorganized,” or where a relationship has really been affected because of it.

I suppose there are times I feel scattered just in general, and maybe that could spill over into conversations or making plans, but I can’t point to anything specific and say, yes, that caused a problem with a friend or family member. It’s not something that stands out to me the way the work things do.

So I’d say… not that I’ve clearly noticed. If you mean smaller annoyances, maybe I’d have to think more, but I don’t want to make it sound like there’s been some big relationship issue from it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences cognitive fatigue
doctor.question: Do you feel like your brain gets tired more quickly than it used to when you're trying to think or concentrate?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: I can start going over the day's dry-cleaning orders just fine, but after a few minutes my mind is off on labels, choir plans, or something at home, and then I realize I missed half of what I was supposed to check.
target_item.reason: The question is about mental fatigue while trying to think or concentrate, which most directly relates to difficulty sustaining attention over time.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think so, though I don’t know if I would have described it as “tired” at first. It’s more like my mind starts out okay, and then it just sort of drifts off before I realize it.

Like at the dry-cleaning place, I can sit down or stand there and start going over the day’s orders just fine. I’ll be checking what needs to be done, matching things up, looking at the tags or the labels, and for the first few minutes I feel like, okay, I’m doing it. But then somehow my mind has wandered off to something else — maybe I’m thinking about a label on one garment, and then that reminds me of something else, or I start thinking about choir plans, or something I need to handle at home. And then I come back to what I’m supposed to be doing and realize I’ve missed half of what I was supposed to check.

So it’s not always that I feel sleepy or physically exhausted. It’s more that concentrating doesn’t hold the way I expect it to. I’ll think I’m following along, but then I notice I’ve been somewhere else in my head. And that does feel tiring, because then I have to go back and re-check things, and I’m never quite sure what I actually took in and what I only thought I took in.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences cognitive fatigue as a prominent symptom
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're unable to think clearly or make decisions after a period of mental effort?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: I can start going over the day's dry-cleaning orders just fine, but after a few minutes my mind is off on labels, choir plans, or something at home, and then I realize I missed half of what I was supposed to check.
target_item.reason: The question asks about trouble thinking clearly or making decisions after mental effort, which most directly maps to difficulty sustaining attention and concentration over time.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think that’s a fair way to put it, though for me it feels less like I suddenly can’t think at all and more like everything gets kind of… slippery. Like I can start out with the dry-cleaning orders and be perfectly able to follow what I’m supposed to do. I’ll be looking at the tickets, checking what’s come in, what needs to be matched up, what’s ready, what still needs attention — and at the beginning I feel like I’m clear enough.

But after a few minutes, it’s like my mind doesn’t stay with it. I’ll be looking at a label, and then that label makes me think of something else, or my mind jumps to choir plans, or something I’m supposed to do at home, and I don’t always notice right away that I’ve left the task in my head. Then I sort of come back and realize I’ve missed half of what I was supposed to be checking.

That’s when decisions get harder, because I’m not sure what I actually already looked at and what I only thought I looked at. So I might have to go back over the same order again, and then I get more unsure because now I’m trying to remember, “Did I check this already? Did I match that up right?” It’s not that I don’t know how to do the work. It’s that after holding my attention on it for a bit, my thinking doesn’t feel as clean or steady.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in social relationships due to their symptoms
doctor.question: Have you noticed your difficulties with organization and focus affecting your relationships with family or friends?

target_item.reason: The question asks specifically about effects on relationships with family or friends, but the provided symptom profile only documents impairment at work and church, not clear personal relationship impairment.

patient.answer:
I honestly don’t know that I can say yes to that in any clear way. With family or friends, I can’t think of someone telling me, you know, “You never pay attention,” or “Your organization is causing problems between us,” or anything like that.

I mean, I’m sure I have moments where I’m a little scattered or where I’m not as on top of things as I’d like to be, but I don’t have a specific relationship problem that comes to mind. It’s easier for me to notice it in more structured settings, where there are tasks and things that have to be done a certain way. With family and friends, it’s a little more vague, I guess.

So… no, not that I’ve really noticed. If it’s happening in small ways, maybe I’m not picking up on it, but I wouldn’t want to say it’s been a major issue because I don’t really have an example of that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in social relationships due to their symptoms
doctor.question: Have you felt like your difficulties with organization and focus have significantly affected your ability to maintain or deepen relationships with friends or family?

target_item.reason: The question asks specifically about impact on maintaining or deepening relationships with friends or family, but the provided symptom profile does not include a clear family/friend relationship impairment example; the prior answer also denied noticing such an effect.

patient.answer:
I don’t think I can really say that it has, at least not in a significant way. I mean, when you say “maintain or deepen relationships,” that sounds like a pretty big thing, like losing friends or not being close to family because I can’t stay organized or focused, and I don’t really have an example like that.

With work tasks, it’s easier for me to see where I get scattered, because there are orders and labels and steps, and if I lose track, there’s something concrete that shows it. But with friends or family, it’s harder for me to measure. I still talk to people, I still show up in the ways I know how, and I can’t think of anyone saying I’ve pulled away or that I’m impossible to deal with because of being disorganized.

I’m not saying I’m perfect. I’m sure there are times I forget little things or I’m not as present as I should be, but I don’t know that I’d connect that to relationships not growing or falling apart. So… no, not that I’ve noticed in any clear or major way.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in social relationships due to their symptoms
doctor.question: Have you felt like your difficulties with organization and focus have caused you significant distress or problems in your relationships with others?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: The shop has had late orders, confused billing, and tense moments with staff and customers, and at church I have stepped back from leading some planning because people were getting frustrated with me.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether organization and focus difficulties have caused significant distress or problems in relationships with others, which is best covered by the functional impairment profile describing tense moments with staff and customers and frustration at church.

patient.answer:
Yes… when you put it that way, I think it has caused problems, more than I maybe wanted to admit at first. I was thinking mostly about family and friends before, but with “relationships with others,” that does include work and church, and that’s where I can see it more clearly.

At the shop, it has definitely created tension. If I lose track of an order or don’t keep the steps straight, then an order can end up late, or the billing can get confused, and then it’s not just some private mistake in my head — somebody else has to deal with it. A customer is upset, or a coworker is trying to figure out what I meant, or we’re all going back through something that should have been simple. And I feel awful when that happens, because I’m not trying to be careless. I’m trying to do it right, but when I get disorganized, it can make other people frustrated with me.

There have been tense moments with staff and customers because of that. Not constant screaming or anything like that, but you can feel it — people get short, or they’re watching me more closely, or I feel like I have to explain myself. And then I get embarrassed, because I know they need me to be dependable.

At church, too, I’ve stepped back from leading some planning things because people were getting frustrated with me. That was hard, because I care about being involved, and I like helping, but keeping all the planning details straight was becoming a problem. I could tell it was wearing on people, and I didn’t want to be the reason things got confusing or delayed.

So yes, I would say it’s caused distress. Maybe not so much in my closest family relationships, but with coworkers, customers, and people at church, yes — it has affected how comfortable I feel and how much responsibility I’m willing to take on.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant emotional distress due to their difficulties
doctor.question: Do you often feel sad or depressed because of your difficulties with organization and focus?

target_item.reason: The question asks about feeling sad or depressed due to organization and focus difficulties, but the provided symptom profile does not include a depression or mood symptom item.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d call it sad or depressed, exactly. I mean, I do get upset with myself sometimes, and embarrassed, especially when I feel like I should have been able to keep something straight and I didn’t. There’s that feeling of, “Why can’t I just do this the way other people seem to do it?” But I don’t know if that rises to the level of feeling depressed.

It’s more like frustration, I guess. Or discouragement in the moment. If I make a mistake or things get disorganized, I can really stew on it for a while, and I feel bad because I don’t want people thinking I don’t care or that I’m not trying. But I wouldn’t say I’m walking around sad all the time because of it.

So… often sad or depressed? I don’t think so. Frustrated and disappointed in myself sometimes, yes. But depressed doesn’t feel like quite the right word for it.
